n: Chapter 16 is Ezekiel’s longest prophecy—an allegory of Jerusalem as an abandoned baby girl whom God rescues, raises, and marries, but who becomes unfaithful. Its language is blunt because covenant betrayal is serious.

f.w: Again the word of the LORD came unto me

n: Ezekiel’s task is to make Jerusalem face honestly what she has done.

f.w: cause Jerusalem to know her abominations

n: Jerusalem was originally a Canaanite city (it was a Jebusite town before David took it). Calling her parents an Amorite and a Hittite means: by nature, you are no better than the pagans around you.

f.w: thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite
f.g: Amorites and Hittites were among the peoples of Canaan before Israel.

n: At birth the baby received none of the ordinary care: no cutting of the cord, no washing, no rubbing with salt (a common ancient practice), no wrapping in cloths.

f.g: Newborns were rubbed with salt, thought to cleanse and strengthen the skin.
Wrapped snugly in strips of cloth.

n: No one cared enough to do these things. The newborn was thrown out into an open field to die—a cruel practice known in the ancient world.

f.w: cast out in the open field
f.g: Infant exposure—abandoning unwanted babies.

n: God passed by, saw her struggling in her own blood, and said, “Live!” twice. This is grace: life given to someone who could do nothing for herself.
Under God’s care she grew like a plant in the field and matured into a young woman—Israel grew from a small family in Egypt into a nation.

f.w: I have caused thee to multiply

n: When she came of age, God spread his garment over her—a sign of marriage and protection—and made a covenant with her. This represents the covenant at Sinai: “thou becamest mine.”

f.w: I spread my skirt over thee
f.g: A symbolic act of betrothal and protection.

f.w: entered into a covenant with thee

n: He washed and anointed her. Washing and anointing are covenant images that also suggest preparation for holy service.

f.w: I throughly washed away thy blood

n: He dressed her in embroidered clothing, fine leather sandals, linen, and costly fabric—the language even echoes the materials of the tabernacle.

f.g: Fine leather—the same material used to cover the tabernacle.
Embroidered cloth.

n: He adorned her with bracelets and a necklace, like a bride.
A nose ring, earrings, and a beautiful crown completed her royal adornment.

f.g: Literally a nose ring, a common bridal ornament.

n: She ate the finest food and became exceedingly beautiful, rising to be a kingdom—the glory years of David and Solomon.

f.w: thou didst prosper into a kingdom

n: Her fame spread among the nations, but her beauty was a gift—perfect because of the splendor God had given her.

f.w: my comeliness, which I had put upon thee
f.g: Her beauty came from God, not from herself.

n: The turning point: she trusted in her own beauty instead of the Giver and gave herself to every passerby. In the prophets, prostitution symbolizes idolatry—giving to false gods the love owed to God.

f.w: thou didst trust in thine own beauty

n: She used the very clothing God gave her to decorate idol shrines—turning gifts against the Giver. Such a thing should never have happened.

f.g: Various colors.

n: She melted down her gold and silver jewelry—God’s gifts—to make idols in human form.

f.g: Male idols.

f.w: of my gold and of my silver

n: She clothed these idols with her embroidered garments and offered them God’s oil and incense.

f.g: Offerings that belonged to God.

n: Even the food God provided she offered to idols as a pleasing aroma.
Worst of all, she sacrificed the children she had borne to God—a horrific practice of Molech worship. Were her other betrayals not enough?

f.w: thy sons and thy daughters, whom thou hast borne unto me

n: God calls them “my children”—the children of his covenant—slain and offered in fire to idols.

f.w: to cause them to pass through the fire

n: In all this she forgot where she came from—the helpless, abandoned baby God had saved. Forgetting God’s past mercy leads to ingratitude and sin.

f.w: thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth

n: God breaks in with a cry of grief: “Woe, woe to you!”

f.g: A cry of lament as much as of judgment.

n: She built a shrine-platform and set up high places in every public street.

f.g: A raised mound or platform, probably for idol worship.

n: Idol shrines stood at every crossroads, and she offered herself to all who passed—her idolatry was open and constant.

f.w: at every head of the way
f.g: At the beginning of every road or intersection.

n: She made alliances with Egypt, adopting its gods—treaties with nations meant honoring their deities, so foreign politics became spiritual unfaithfulness.

f.g: A crude image of Egypt’s power and allure.

n: So God reduced her territory and handed her to her enemies, the Philistines—who were themselves embarrassed by her conduct.

f.g: Reduced her allotted portion or territory.
Philistine cities; even pagans were ashamed of Judah’s behavior.

n: She also courted Assyria, yet never felt satisfied. Idolatry never fills the emptiness it promises to fill.

f.g: Never satisfied.

n: She extended her unfaithfulness to Babylon (Chaldea), still unsatisfied.

f.g: Babylon.

n: “How weak your heart is!”—her will had no strength to resist temptation; she acted like a brazen, domineering woman.

f.g: Possibly “how feverish/lovesick your heart is.”
Bold and shameless.

n: She built shrines at every crossroads, yet unlike a prostitute she did not even charge a fee.

f.g: She refused payment.

n: She is like an adulterous wife who prefers strangers to her own husband.
Prostitutes are paid, but Jerusalem pays her lovers! Judah actually sent tribute to foreign powers to win their favor.

f.w: thou givest thy gifts to all thy lovers

n: She is the reverse of other women: she pays instead of being paid. Her folly is beyond reason.

f.g: You are the opposite.

n: Now comes the verdict: “Hear the word of the LORD.”

f.g: A stark title for covenant-breaking Jerusalem.

n: Because of her shameful idolatry, her lovers, her idols, and the blood of her children…

f.g: Possibly “wealth” or “lust”; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

n: …God will gather all her former lovers and enemies against her and expose her shame publicly. The nations she trusted would be the ones to destroy her.

f.w: I will gather all thy lovers

n: She will be judged under the law as an adulteress and murderer—both crimes carried the death penalty.

f.w: women that break wedlock and shed blood

n: Her shrines will be torn down, and she will be stripped of the finery God gave her, left as she was at the beginning.
A crowd will stone her and cut her down—the legal punishment for adultery and idolatry, here carried out by invading armies.

f.w: they shall stone thee with stones

n: Her houses will be burned before the watching nations. Then her unfaithfulness will end.

f.w: they shall burn thine houses with fire

n: Then God’s fury will rest; his jealousy will turn away, and he will be calm. Judgment has a limit.

f.w: my jealousy shall depart from thee

n: Because she forgot her youth and provoked God, he will bring her conduct back on her own head.

f.g: Provoked or enraged me.

n: A proverb: “Like mother, like daughter.” Jerusalem has become just like the pagan peoples she came from.

f.w: As is the mother, so is her daughter
f.g: The second section of the chapter compares Jerusalem to her “sisters.”

n: Like her pagan “mother” and “sisters,” she despised her husband and children.

f.w: that lotheth her husband and her children
f.g: Who rejected her covenant God and sacrificed her children.

n: Her “older sister” is Samaria, the fallen northern kingdom to the north; her “younger sister” is Sodom to the south. (Facing east, left is north and right is south.)

f.g: Capital of the northern kingdom, destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC.

n: Jerusalem didn’t merely copy them; she quickly became even more corrupt.

f.w: as if that were a very little thing
f.g: As if their sins were too small for her.

n: God swears that Sodom never did as much evil as Jerusalem has. Greater knowledge makes sin more serious.

f.w: Sodom thy sister hath not done

n: Sodom’s sins included pride, overabundance, careless ease, and refusing to help the poor and needy. This verse shows that neglecting the poor was among the roots of Sodom’s destruction.

f.w: pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness

n: They were arrogant and did detestable things before God, so he removed them.
Samaria didn’t commit half Jerusalem’s sins. By comparison, Jerusalem makes her sisters look righteous.

f.g: Made them seem righteous in comparison.

n: Jerusalem, who once looked down on her sisters, must now bear her own shame. Judging others while sinning ourselves is a dangerous blindness.

f.g: Put to shame.

n: A surprising promise: God will restore the fortunes of Sodom and Samaria—and of Jerusalem along with them.

f.w: When I shall bring again their captivity
f.g: Restore their fortunes.

n: Being restored alongside those she despised will humble Jerusalem; it will comfort her sisters to see that she was no better.

f.w: in that thou art a comfort unto them
f.g: Her greater sin makes them feel less judged.

n: All three sisters will return to their former state. The promise points to a restoration bigger than Israel alone.
In her proud days Jerusalem used Sodom as a byword of wickedness, never thinking of her own sins.

f.w: was not mentioned by thy mouth
f.g: Or “was a byword in your mouth.”

n: That was before her own wickedness was exposed—now she is mocked by Syria, the Philistines, and her neighbors.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “Edom,” which differs from “Aram” (Syria) by one similar Hebrew letter.

n: Jerusalem must bear the consequences of her lewdness and abominations.

f.g: You are bearing the results.

n: God will deal with her as she dealt with him: she treated her covenant oath with contempt and broke it.

f.w: despised the oath in breaking the covenant

n: The great turn: “Nevertheless.” God will remember the covenant he made with her in her youth and establish an everlasting covenant. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the restored new and everlasting covenant.
Remembering her ways, she will be ashamed. She will receive her “sisters” as daughters—not because they were part of the old covenant, but through God’s new grace.

f.g: Not because of Jerusalem’s own faithfulness, but by God’s gift.

n: God will establish his covenant, and she will know he is the LORD.

f.w: I will establish my covenant with thee

n: When God forgives her completely, she will be humbled into silence. Forgiveness does not make sin trivial; it leads to deep gratitude and humility.

f.w: when I am pacified toward thee
f.g: When I have made atonement for you (Hebrew kipper).
